en: Who knows? We do not know if it is true:
Much is false and much is true;
No one has come back having seen it.
Unless God knows it plainly,
Half is false and half is true;
No person has come back from its side.
Unless the Creator himself knows,
It appears on those two nights;
At the base of its two humps
A naked child rides, they say.
The flat-humped black camel
Still lives today, they say.
For those it has truly touched,
To Khan Manas's tomb
It comes each Friday, they say.
A mortal whom God loves
Sees it plainly, they say.
After sacrificing Zhelmayyan,
The halter his mother had entrusted to him—
After the boy had taken it for her,
As he rode onward,
At Jangyryk's Zhar-Kyya,
On a trail for beasts in single file,
His roaring split the stones,
His shouting split the head.
The horse beneath him had grown thin;
He himself had grown terribly old.
Lamenting, telling his sorrow,
Disgraced in his final years,
Herding camels, to the plain
He longed to come just once.
His beard had whitened like a swan;
His eyes had reddened like a raven's.
His joints had grown loose;
His eyes had begun to fester;
His chest had begun to wheeze;
His whole body shook.
Twelve limbs and eighty bones
Trembled without ceasing.
His neck bones stood out long;
His eyes were red like a raven's.
Disgraced, herding camels,
The nobleman's orphaned son
He yearned to see just once,
Left in disgrace.
For twelve full years
That man had herded camels.
When his horse could go no farther,
That man herded them on foot.
Grieving, aching, his strength gone,
His coat worn out and hanging loose,
He had grown old.
His strength gone, slumping,
He had grown thin.
His imposing presence gone, dragging along,
He had fallen into misery.
His wits fled, his strength gone,
He was no longer himself.
Taking snuff and working himself up,
He beat the camel in front,
Muttering, “May you be left without an owner!”
When he climbed a little hill,
Semetey saw him again.
A goatskin coat on his body,
That man herding camels,
Leather trousers on his backside,
His beard white,
With little time left—in that year
He was near the time of death.
The mount beneath him
Had lost its mane and tail;
He rode a gray, short-tailed horse.
That year Koktulpar
Had fallen into ill repute.
Never resting in winter,
Nor grazing enough in summer,
It had lost its mane entirely.
Upon it Bakay grieved,
What you see today is gone tomorrow.
Alas, such is this world of shit!
The marten-fur cap upon his head—
Who has not worn it with a swagger?
With fortune resting on his head,
Who has not gone about thundering?
When they heard Bakay's name,
The Chinese people beyond the mountains trembled.
To Bakay, touched by Khizir,
Back when Manas was alive,
No one came without ablution.
In former times, once upon a time,
King Bakay, that dear hero—
That day Bakay was sorely diminished.
If you ask about his earlier days,
The mount beneath him,
With red mane, with gray mane,
Was the resplendent Koktulpar.
It had lost its mane and tail,
But had not yet fallen into ill repute,
Had not yet received the name Kokcholok.
Herding camels, bellowing much,
He had ridden up onto a hill.
It was not Kokcholok—it was Bakay
Himself who had fallen into ill repute.
Up onto the hill, howling,
A man came to a halt.
Calling all the camels ownerless,
A man cursed them roundly.
“Where has half of this herd gone?”
A man then asked, missing them.
“Where is the gray male camel?”
A man looked about.
Beating all the camels,
A man went striking them.
“May you pile up on every hill!
May flies strike you and wipe you out!
Oh, as though Semetey had come today,
As though you had seen my orphan,
Your knees bending,
You ownerless wretches, running toward the foothills!
This year you have not grazed the foothill grass,
Have not drunk water on the plain,
Nor gone along the woods.
It has now been twelve full years
Since you cropped this birch.
All these years you have not come,
You beasts left without an owner,
Nor eaten your fill of tamarisk.
Since Manas, my joy, died,
You have not seen the willow tops.
This year, beasts kept penned away,
How many years has it been?
For Bakay to tend you, bellowing in grief—
How many years has it been?”
Cursing the camels, Khan Bakay
Turned Kokcholok's head.
Telling his sorrow to God,
Leopard Bakay stood there:
“While Khan Manas lived,
Why did I not die then?
Herding camels after him,
Why could I not avoid being left behind?
The marten-fur cap upon my head—
Is this the day it turns to grass?
My ruin, compared with my joy—
Is this the day it grows greater?
My wings broken,
Parted from Khan Manas,
Grieving, herding camels,
Torments no person has seen—
Is this my day to bear them?
With my beard white,
With my journey ahead,
My eyes reddening like a raven's,
At the time when I might die,
Not dying, herding camels,
I am fated to die a wretched death.
Bellowing in the open wilderness,
I am fated to die a wretched death.
Unable to manage these beasts,
I am fated to be left on a mountain pass.
I am fated to be left upon the earth.
Alas, Manas, if only you had not died!
Bakay, if only you had not known humiliation!
When my joints have failed,
Herding camels, I have been disgraced.
Such grief as this—
God, if you have created a living soul,
Do not give it to your mortal.
The humiliation I have seen—
From now on, one God,
Aged as I am,
May old men never see it!
When I was in my full strength,
When my Magnanimous Manas lived,
Why did I not die then?
Dark, looming Great Beijing—
When I held it under siege,
Making the Chinese crack and crash,
When I was beating them,
Why did I not die then?
Looming like Ala-Too,
When I was resplendent,
Going to holy war and clashing,
The Muslims' golden banner—
When I held it,
Those who roused my wrath—
When I held them captive,
Those who truly angered me—
When I beat them,
When my strength was great,
When my blue-maned wolf was alive,
Why did I not die then?!
Zulpukor from my wrist—
In the days when I hung it there,
The eighteen thousand worlds—
In the days when I ruled them,
Havoc upon the face of the earth—
In the days when I brought it,
Six thousand otter pelts, a thousand silver ingots,
Crushing them, for my tribute,
In the days when I took it,
Across the face of the earth like a falcon—
In the days when I swept,
A piercing battle cry at the unbelievers—
In the days when I hurled it,
Why did I not die then?
I have herded camels in disgrace.
My lord Manas, take me with you!”
So saying, Khan Bakay then
Turned Kokcholok's head.
Speaking of his sorrow, brave Bakay
Now stood bellowing and weeping.
Speaking of his loss, mighty Bakay
Grieved most bitterly.
Wanting to die, but unable to die,
Unable to take his own life,
Khan Bakay was no longer himself.
Hill upon hill, a little hill—
He stopped on a little hill.
Those ownerless beasts before him—
He looked for the missing ownerless beasts.
That one a young camel, that a fifth-year female,
That one a gelded camel, a young male,
As he looked over the mature camels,
Bakay suffered once again.
Now he turned Kokcholok's head;
As though his people had fallen into ruin,
Bakay stood bellowing now:
“Perish, you and your feast!
Why did I turn toward their feast?!
Let me eat a bullet instead of feast food!
I have lost my camels.
Perish, you and your funeral feast!
Why did I turn toward that feast?
Let me eat stones instead of food!
It was a beast left by Manas;
I have lost Zhelmayyan!
Its gray male companion is missing,
The gray female is missing with it,
Zhelmayyan is missing too.
Parted from Zhelmayyan,
White-bearded Bakay has no fortune!
You cursed, dim eyes,
Have you been gouged out?
You beard fit to be burned,
Have you been shorn today?
Good heavens, when the orphan comes tomorrow,
When he asks, ‘Where is Zhelmayyan?’
What torment shall I bear?
You beard fit to be shorn,
What answer shall I give?
What shall I do about that suffering?
With a golden halter on its head,
Bringing on misfortune like this,
My dear child Kanykey
Left it in my keeping!”
